HYPERTHERMIA 
 
 
 
GENERAL APPROACH 
 
•
Clinical features: Decreased GCS, agitation, sweating (no sweating in heat stroke) 
•
ECG Features: Non-specific ST and T changes, tachycardia, features of electrolyte AbNs, VT 
and VF can occur 
•
Triage to RESUS AREA, CENTRAL TEMPERATURE MONITORING 
•
Rapid ABC assessment, 2 IV lines, monitors, HGT, VBG, urine ßHCG, ECG 
•
Consider early airway management for altered GCS/seizures 
•
Benzodiazepines for seizures/agitation 
•
Correct electrolyte abnormalities & HGT 
•
Crystalloid fluid bolus 20mg/kg if hypotensive 
•
Comprehensive history and exam, including: 
§
Circumstances that patient was found in – precipitating event, outside/inside, 
downtime if known 
§
Co-morbidities, chronic medications, symptoms prior to arrival 
§
History of trauma or intoxication à  NB! TOXIDROME FEATURES 
•
Document specific features and severity of hyperthermia 
•
Further investigations: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFTs, INR, Paracetamol/Salicylate level, urine tox 
screen, imaging as clinically indicated 
 
NB – THERE IS OFTEN AN UNDERLYING MEDICAL CONDITION CONTRIBUTING TO HYPERTHERMIA 
ACTIVE COOLING 
TARGET Temp < 39°C WITHIN 30 MINUTES 
•
Peripheral cooling  
Ice bath immersion, cold wet sheet, ice packs in groin/axillae, fan cooling, air conditioner 
•
Central cooling 
Cold IV fluids, usually peripheral measures are effective 
•
Intubation: Avoid scoline – risk of hyperkalaemia 
•
Avoid antipyretics – NSAIDs and aspirin not effective 
•
May develop fulminant hepatic failure, multi-organ dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, 
sepsis, AKI – manage supportively 
CAUSES and DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS 
 
§
Environmental exposure – outdoor sports, marathons 
§
Toxins – anticholinergic, sympathomimetic 
§
Sepsis  
§
Extremes of age – poor thermoregulation 
§
Endocrine – hyperthyroid, thyroid storm, phaeochromocytoma 
§
Serotonin syndrome 
§
Malignant hyperthermia 
§
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome 
§
Hypothalamic dysfunction – trauma, stroke, CNS infection 
DEFINITIONS 
 
Minor heat illness  
muscle cramps, minor peripheral oedema, syncope, 
heat rash 
 
Heat exhaustion 
Temp < 40°C, sweating intact 
Intact neurological function, weakness, fatigue, 
headache, nausea, vomiting, syncope 
 
ABOVE CAN BE MANAGED WITH SUPPORTIVE CARE 
 
Heat stroke 
Temp > 40°C, ± sweating   
Agitation, confusion, seizures, coma, shock, AKI, 
coagulopathy, electrolyte disturbances 
 
HEAT STROKE IS A LIFE-THREATENING EMERGENCY! 
Dr du Plessis / Dr R Gihwala CMJAH Emergency Department June 2020
